pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** What happens when things collide

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** no general KS2 'energy' topic (energy enters at KS3), so no direct UK primary statutory match; nearest UK home is KS2 'Working scientifically' (asking questions, making and testing predictions) and forces work on collisions/changes in motion.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NATIONAL (NGSS): 4-PS3-3 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'; clarification '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'; DCI PS3.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; assessment boundary excludes quantitative measurements of energy. NGSS-anchored. Sits directly on 'Speed and energy' (faster = more kinetic energy).

- **Operational details:** Children ask questions and predict outcomes about the energy changes when objects collide: energy transfers from one object to another (one speeds up, the other slows), and some energy also goes to the surroundings as sound and a little warming. Strictly qualitative and observational — no momentum, no calculations; the emphasis (per NGSS) is on the energy change [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3].

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 9-10).
bestPractices: Lead with predict-then-observe: before each collision the child predicts what will happen to BOTH objects ('which speeds up? which slows? will there be a sound?'), then runs it and compares — the gap is where the energy-transfer idea forms.

Use clean, watchable collisions — a rolling marble hitting a stationary one (Newton's-cradle / boules style), a fast ball hitting a slow one — so the transfer (giver slows, receiver speeds up) is directly visible.

Make the surroundings audible/visible: name the BANG and any warming as energy that left the moving objects — 'the click you hear is some of the energy leaving as sound' — which seeds conservation without the formal law.
Keep attention on energy/speed change, not force (the NGSS clarification is explicit): describe what happens to each object's motion and where the energy went, not how hard they pushed.
Vary the incoming speed and connect back to 'speed and energy': a faster striker transfers more (knocks the target further, louder click), reinforcing more-speed-more-energy.
keyRepresentations: Two-ball collision: a moving ball striking a stationary one (giver slows/stops, receiver moves off) — the canonical transfer picture.
Before/after speed arrows on each object (long arrow = fast, short = slow) showing motion handed from one to the other.
A 'where did the energy go?' tally: into the other object (motion) + a bit to the surroundings (sound + slight warming).
Everyday anchors: snooker/pool break, bumper cars, a kicked ball striking another, skittles/bowling.
commonMisconceptions: 'The energy just disappears when things stop after a crash' — the central energy-is-lost error; it transferred to the other object and to the surroundings (sound, warming), it didn't vanish.
Thinking only ONE object changes — children watch the target and ignore that the striker slowed down too.
Treating the sound of the collision as separate/irrelevant rather than as energy carried away from the moving objects.
Reasoning about which object 'wins' or 'pushes harder' (forces) instead of how the energy/speed changes — the NGSS clarification steers away from force talk here.
'The bigger/heavier object always keeps moving and the small one always stops' — outcome depends on speeds and masses together; predict-then-test surfaces the surprises.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: children ask questions and predict outcomes about the energy changes when objects collide. When objects collide, energy can transfer from one to another (often one speeds up while the other slows, though in a head-on crash both may slow or stop). Some energy also leaves the moving objects to the surroundings as sound and a little warming (and into squashing when objects deform), so it is redistributed, never destroyed. Keep everything qualitative and observational (NGSS 4-PS3-3): no momentum, no calculations, and emphasis on the energy change [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3] forces. The core predict-then-observe cycle and 'where did the energy go?' bookkeeping can run as a live screen simulation, with real marbles/physical collisions, or as reference/assessment companions; each is described below with its affordances and limits.

activities.title: Collision lab: predict, run, and track where the energy goes
feedback: If a learner says the energy 'disappeared', point to the target that moved off and the 'surroundings' bar: whether the striker slowed, stopped, or bounced back, 'the click you hear is some of the energy leaving as sound' — it moved, it didn't vanish.
If a learner watches only the target and ignores the striker, replay and ask them to describe what happened to the striker's speed too.
When a faster striker knocks the target further with a louder click, name it: more incoming speed carried more energy to transfer.
activities.rationale: A live predict-then-test interaction where the learner sets the speed, commits a prediction, then sees per-object motion arrows and energy bars update makes the transfer visible and answers 'where did the energy go?' directly. Optional interaction cues — speed sliders, size/mass toggle, before/after motion arrows (long = fast, short = slow), motion bars handing energy across, and a small surroundings bar gaining the sound+warming share — make the energy-bookkeeping mechanism concrete and let surprises (e.g. a lighter striker rebounding) emerge from the child's own prediction. Keep it bars-and-arrows, never numbers, to stay inside the qualitative Tier-A boundary.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-3 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'); clarification emphasises energy change due to speed change, NOT forces; DCI PS3.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; boundary excludes quantitative energy.
Children commonly believe energy 'disappears' when colliding objects stop, and attend to only one object; the sound/warming of a collision is energy carried to the surroundings.
learnerActions: Choose incoming speed in a simulation, or release the same marble from different heights on a fixed ramp and observe its speed before a stationary target. Keep objects,surface and collision alignment unchanged for the speed comparison; explore a mass toggle separately.
COMMIT a prediction before running: say what each object will do ('the red one will stop, the blue one will shoot off') AND predict whether there will be a sound.

Observe both objects. In a nearly elastic,head-on equal-mass model with one target initially still, the striker nearly stops as the target moves off; with different masses or materials it may continue or rebound. Record the actual outcome rather than requiring every real collision to match one ideal case.
Watch the energy bookkeeping: the striker's motion-bar shrinks as the target's grows, and a small 'surroundings' bar lights up for the sound and slight warming, so the total is visibly accounted for.

Vary incoming speed while keeping the same objects,alignment and surface. A faster incoming object carries more kinetic energy; observe how much reaches target motion,sound,deformation or warming, rather than guaranteeing a particular loudness or travel distance.
activities.intendedInsight: When things collide, energy doesn't disappear when the striker slows: it moves into the other object and some escapes to the surroundings as sound and a little warming. More incoming speed means more energy transferred.

activities.title: Watch real clean collisions and name where the energy went
feedback: Track the changed motion and listen for sound or look for deformation. Warming may be too small to detect by touch,so do not require a child to feel it; use the labelled model to discuss possible internal-energy changes.
If a learner thinks the still marble 'can't gain energy', have them predict and watch the struck marble shoot off: energy was transferred to it, which is why it moves.
Name the BANG explicitly as energy that left the moving objects, seeding conservation without the formal law.
activities.rationale: Clean, watchable physical collisions make the transfer (giver slows, receiver speeds up) directly visible and let learners use their own ears for the sound share. The head-on case is a strong challenge to the 'energy disappears' idea, clearest with squashy balls that visibly stop and squash (any thud is sound energy, and warming may be too small to feel); with hard marbles that rebound, motion remains and the click still evidences some energy leaving. Physical objects give a tactile, audible experience; this complements the screen model rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Children commonly believe energy 'disappears' when colliding objects stop, and attend to only one object; the sound/warming of a collision is energy carried to the surroundings.

4-PS3-3 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'); clarification emphasises energy change due to speed change, NOT forces; DCI PS3.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; boundary excludes quantitative energy.
learnerActions: Roll one marble into a stationary one (Newton's-cradle / boules style) and watch the giver slow or stop while the receiver moves off.

Use two identical balls of equal mass approaching head-on at equal speeds. Predict their motion before testing: hard,nearly elastic balls tend to rebound,while soft sticky clay balls may join and stop near the collision point. The materials and conditions matter; do not generalise this outcome to unequal masses.
Close your eyes during the head-on crash and listen: what do you HEAR? Discuss what that sound tells you about where the energy went.

Make a 'where did the energy go?' tally for each collision: any motion that remains or is passed to the other object + some to the surroundings (sound you hear, plus possible slight warming that may be too small to feel) + any squashing (deformation). For sticky clay balls that stop, most of the motion energy goes into squashing and warming rather than motion.
Try everyday anchors — snooker/pool break, bumper cars, a kicked ball striking another, skittles/bowling — and describe the transfer each time.
activities.intendedInsight: When objects rebound,some energy remains as motion; when soft objects stop and deform,more of the initial motion energy becomes internal energy or deformation. Sound may carry some energy to the surroundings. Account for all these destinations rather than treating lost motion as destroyed energy.

activities.title: Predict outcomes and trace the energy (check/assess companion)
feedback: If a learner says energy disappeared,compare the motion before and after,list any sound or deformation,and discuss possible internal-energy changes. Rebounding objects retain motion energy; any warming may be too small to feel. Include the surroundings when accounting for the total.
If a learner predicts the outcome from size alone, remind them the outcome depends on BOTH speed and mass — a fast small object can carry more energy than a slow big one; vary both.
If a learner says the still marble can't gain energy, point back to the struck object shooting off as evidence of transfer.
activities.rationale: Prediction and matching formats map naturally onto the standard's 'predict outcomes' verb and surface whether a learner tracks energy to all destinations. These formats are used to check and consolidate; on their own they assess recognition and prediction rather than eliciting the hands-on predict-then-run cycle, so pair them with Activity 1 or 2.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-3 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-3]'); clarification emphasises energy change due to speed change, NOT forces; DCI PS3.B '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]… [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-2, 4-PS3-3]'; boundary excludes quantitative energy.
learnerActions: Predict post-collision motion: for a given collision, choose what happens to ball B (and to the striker).
Match 'energy went to →' with the destinations: the other object (motion) / sound / warming / squashing (deformation).
Order a set of collisions using the same objects by how much energy the striker brings in (e.g. by incoming speed).
Answer the counterexample: two identical marbles, one still; the moving one stops and the still one goes off at the same speed — did energy disappear, and where did it go?
Answer: after any collision, is the total energy more, less, or the same as before, and where would you look for the 'missing' bit?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can predict outcomes and name all the destinations of the energy, including the surroundings and deformation share, confirming they track energy rather than treat it as lost — the TOTAL energy, including the surroundings, is the same before and after; motion energy is shared between the objects and partly changed into sound, warming or squashing.

activities.title: Before/after reference scene (optional companion)
feedback: Use the flaps to confirm answers after a learner has predicted, rather than revealing them first.
activities.rationale: A static before/after scene with tappable flaps is a fair reference and vocabulary aid. Because it is fixed it cannot deliver the prediction-then-result cycle that builds the idea, so treat it as a companion to the interactive or physical collisions, not a substitute.
learnerActions: Open a before/after collision illustration with tappable 'what happened to each object' and 'where did the energy go' flaps.
Use it to review the canonical two-ball transfer picture and the surroundings share after doing the live or physical activity.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear before/after picture consolidates the vocabulary of transfer and the destinations of the energy as a reference.

constraints: Keep it strictly qualitative and observational: no momentum, no calculations, bars-and-arrows rather than numbers (NGSS assessment boundary excludes quantitative energy).
Keep attention on the energy/speed change and where the energy went, NOT on force or which object 'pushed harder' — the NGSS clarification is explicit on this.
Always attend to BOTH objects: children tend to watch the target and miss that the striker slowed too.
Outcome depends on speed and mass together; avoid 'the bigger/heavier object always keeps moving' — vary both and use predict-then-test to surface surprises.

For an ideal elastic,head-on collision into a stationary target,an equal-mass striker stops,a lighter striker rebounds,and a heavier striker continues. Real materials,rotation,friction and alignment change outcomes; label the model and accept actual observations rather than enforcing its exact prediction.

For the head-on 'both stop' demonstration use squashy/inelastic balls (modelling clay); hard, elastic marbles rebound rather than stop. In either case the click and any warmth/squashing show energy transferred, not destroyed — do not present 'equal marbles stop dead' as the only correct head-on outcome.
Recognition/matching formats check prediction and vocabulary but do not elicit the independent predict-run-observe construction; pair them with hands-on or live collisions.
The static before/after scene is a reference scaffold: it cannot run the prediction-then-result cycle and should follow, not replace, active collisions.

Label the screen simulation as a simplified model. Real marbles or clay allow observing motion,sound and sometimes deformation; slight warming may not be detectable by touch. Model bars represent energy accounting,not a direct measurement or proof that every predicted channel was observed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists the IOP Spark children's-ideas claim as verified:false; the related 'energy disappears / only one object' misconception guidance should be treated as plausible but unverified.

Original error corrected: the original assessment stated two identical marbles colliding head-on at equal speeds 'both stop dead'. For elastic marbles the realistic outcome is to rebound; stopping dead requires inelastic (squashy) objects. Learner-facing text was corrected to hold for either outcome and to use squashy balls where 'stop and squash' is intended, preserving the robust point that sound/warmth/squashing show energy was transferred, not destroyed.

Added correction: the original 'striker stops' picture holds only for equal masses; a lighter striker rebounds off a heavier stationary target. Activity 1 text widened to slow/stop/bounce-back so the mass toggle does not produce a stated outcome that is false.

Comparative efficacy of the live simulation versus physical marbles or the reference scene is not established by the sources; descriptions of fit were softened to affordances/limits, not claims of necessity.

The original row framed force talk as to be avoided per the NGSS clarification; this is a standards-scoping choice for this grade band, retained as a constraint rather than a universal claim that forces are irrelevant to collisions.

assess.poeTask: Set up the head-on case: ask the child to predict what happens when two marbles of equal speed collide head-on — will they bounce back, stop, or pass through — and WHERE the energy goes, before rolling them. The 'energy disappears' child expects it simply gone when they stop; a tracking child predicts the energy leaves as the audible click and slight warmth. Then collide them and listen.
probeDeeper: In the head-on crash, close your eyes — what do you HEAR? What does that sound tell you about where the energy went?
Predict: a fast marble hits a slow, heavy ball. What happens to each, and why?
Counterexample: two identical marbles, one still. The moving one stops and the still one goes off at the same speed. Did energy disappear? Where did it go?
After any collision, is the total energy more, less, or the same as before? Where would you look for the 'missing' bit?
assess.correctAnswer: In the first, the moving marble transfers its kinetic energy to the still one, which speeds off. In the head-on crash both stop, but the energy isn't gone — it's transferred to sound (the click), a little heat, and momentarily squashing the marbles; it moved out of motion into other forms. Energy is transferred, never destroyed, in both.

errorPatterns.pattern: When both objects stop, the energy has just disappeared ('they cancelled out and the energy's gone').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Listen for the sound and feel for warmth; the energy left the kinetic store into sound and thermal — stopping isn't destroying.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both marbles stop, so their energy cancelled out and disappeared.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't name where the energy went when the motion stops.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only the moving object has energy; the still one has none to do anything with ('the still marble is just in the way').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Energy is TRANSFERRED to the struck object — that's why it moves; predict and watch the struck marble shoot off.
errorPatterns.distractor: The still marble can't gain any energy, so it shouldn't move at all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Doesn't expect the struck object to gain energy and move off.

errorPatterns.pattern: The heavier or bigger object always wins the collision, whatever the speeds ('big always beats small').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Outcome depends on BOTH speed and mass — a fast small object can carry more energy than a slow big one; vary both.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the outcome from size alone, ignoring speed.

responseLevels.gap: Says energy disappears when objects stop; thinks only the moving object has energy, or that size alone decides.
responseLevels.full: Tracks kinetic energy transferring between objects and, when motion stops, into sound/heat/deformation (never destroyed), and predicts outcomes using both speed and mass.
responseLevels.partial: Knows energy transfers between colliding objects and predicts simple cases, but says energy is lost when both stop, or ignores sound and heat.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A moving marble hits a still marble and stops; the still one shoots off. Then two marbles crash head-on and BOTH stop dead. In the second case it looks like the energy just vanished. Where did the energy go in each collision?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'both stopped, so the energy disappeared' differs from one who tracks the energy into sound/heat/deformation. The reason tier separates 'energy vanished' from 'energy transferred to sound and heat'.
